Inequality in Education Around the World

Olivia Jiang

November 4, 2026

Introduction

This project examines the differences in educational development and opportunity around the world. The quality of education among a country’s population is a solid indicator of the wellbeing and future advancement of a country, yet it varies significantly across different places and groups of people. I was curious about the extent of these differences, so I turned to the data to find out.

I used data from the United Nations’ Human Development Reports by the UN Development Program; I obtained data from UNDP’s open database which covers 34 years: 1990 to 2023. Note that the variables that I was interested in were missing data past 2023 so the last couple of years (2024 and 2025) aren’t included in my analysis.

The data contains information on the educational attributes of countries’ adults 25 and older.

I’ll focus on the following main measures: the percentage of men and women (individually) with at least secondary education within a country, the average amount of formal education attained by men and women (individually) within a country, and the average amount of education attained by adults within a country. Secondary education, under the UN’s International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED), is defined as an intermediate phase of education spanning ages 11 to 18. The dataset also includes global versions of these measures.

Viewing the global level of education over time

Just as a preliminary look, in this initial plot of the average amount of education worldwide in years, it’s clear that the world is gradually becoming more educated as a whole:

The world’s education level in general has been steadily growing for the past 3 decades from ~5.9 years in 1990 to ~8.8 years in 2023 (a change of ~2.9 years!), which is nice to see. In fact, it has gotten better every year, at a rate of ~0.1 years each year.

However, if we look into how the level of education varies by gender and geographically, some disparities do emerge…

Examining differences by gender

In this plot, when the metric is split by gender, a gap emerges:

The average amount of education for females has never been more than for males. Although they’ve been increasing at very similar speeds — the lines are nearly parallel — there has consistently been a gap of around a year between them. Nonetheless, over the past few years, beginning in 2020, that gap has been shrinking a little; in 2020, the magnitude of the gap dropped to a new low of ~0.8 years, to ~0.7 years in 2021, ~0.7 years in 2022, and ~0.8 years in 2023.

Another way to look at the gender gap is through the percentage of adults in each gender who have at least some level of secondary education:

Again, the percentage of females with education worldwide has never exceeded the percentage of males, with a consistent difference of 9.5 raw percentage points, but this has shrunk to ~8.2 raw percentage points in 2023.
